content.text:
## Why today's Home widget feels weak

- **One HTML file has to do two jobs.** The model writes the full page and a `MONEO_VIEW="widget"` version in the same file, so the widget is an afterthought.
- **There is no fixed size.** The iframe grows from 160 to 560px to fit its content, so cards end up different heights and scroll.
- **You add it blind.** "Add to Home" is just a toggle. You never see the widget among your other cards first.
- **It doesn't look or behave like a real card.** Each one is its own iframe that loads charts from a CDN, shows a skeleton, reloads when the theme changes, and uses slightly different fonts and spacing from Net worth or Briefing.

## Options

| | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Better iframe** | The AI writes separate widget HTML for an exact size (S/M/L), with no scrolling, plus a preview step | Any visual is possible | Still slow, still looks foreign, design quality varies, each widget is a heavy iframe |
| **B. Native templates** *(recommended)* | The AI picks one of about 6 card templates (stat, stat-row, bar-list, trend, progress, list) and links it to saved queries. The app draws it with its own React components | Looks exactly like built-in cards, renders on the server with no iframe, always fits, money is formatted by the app, can be tested | Can't show unusual visuals like a heatmap; we build about 6 components |
| **C. Hybrid** | B by default, with A as a "custom" fallback for what the templates can't do | Most flexible | Two systems to maintain |
| D. Snapshot image | The page is rendered to a PNG on a schedule | — | Data goes stale and it needs a headless browser. Rejected. |

I recommend **B**. Add C only if you find yourself missing a visual. The full artifact page stays HTML; only the Home card goes native.

## How B works

1. You build an artifact as you do now: a full HTML page.
2. You tap **Add to Home**. A small AI call (a few seconds, small JSON output) chooses a template, links it to data, and picks a default size.
3. A preview sheet shows your **real Home** with live data and the new card in place. You can switch S/M/L, and "Tweak the widget" re-runs only the widget step. Nothing is saved until you confirm.
4. On Home it's a normal card with a fixed height and an "Open" link to the full artifact. Edit layout lets you resize and reorder it.

## Architecture

- **The widget spec** is a Zod discriminated union in a new `lib/finance/widget-spec.ts` file, e.g. `{ template: "bar-list", size: "M", title, items: { query: "byCategory", path: "rows", label: "name", value: "total_formatted", bar: "total_minor" } }`.
- **Data:** the widget gets its own saved queries, using the existing `ARTIFACT_SOURCES`, `runArtifactQueries` and date roll-forward. Changing the artifact later never breaks the widget.
- **Checked when saved:** the queries run once and every link must resolve before it can be saved, so a broken widget never reaches Home.
- **Storage:** a new `artifact_widgets` table (artifact_id, spec, queries, size). Since you're the only user, I'd drop the `MONEO_VIEW` widget path and the `fit` iframe code instead of migrating them. Home layout keys stay as `artifact:<id>`.
- **Rendering:** new `components/home-widgets/*` server components using the same `card` styles as the built-ins. Each widget is wrapped in Suspense so a slow query doesn't hold up Home.
- **Sizes:** S, M and L map to 2, 3 and 4 or 6 grid columns with a fixed height. Each template declares which sizes it supports.

## Separately: better full-page design

Instead of just a longer prompt, inject a small **Moneo CSS kit** into every artifact frame (`.m-card`, `.m-stat`, `.m-eyebrow`, `.m-grid`, chart colours) and tell the model to build from it. Pages then match the app by default. The Mercury-style design text in `lib/ai/artifact-examples.ts` should be replaced by this, since it currently fights the app's own look.

## Questions for you

1. B alone, or B with the C escape hatch?
2. Should the widget be generated when you tap Add to Home (my choice, since it's cheaper) or during every artifact build?
3. Should Home cards ever be interactive (e.g. a month toggle), or always read-only with "Open" for more?

content.text:
## What I found: tools and durability

- **The builder can't read everything chat can.** It has 7 read sources. Chat can also read transaction details, entity lists, what-if scenarios, forecasts, wealth (money lent and owed), and agent findings. Net worth history has no tool anywhere, even though Home shows it.
- **It isn't truly durable.** The build runs in `after()` inside one function call with a 300s limit:
  - Closing the tab works only while that call stays alive. A deploy, crash or timeout loses the build, and it gets marked "failed" 6 minutes later.
  - It never retries.
  - When you come back you see only "running". The steps it already showed are gone.

**Fix:**
- **Move the builder to Vercel Workflow.** The repo already uses it for reviews, bank sync and imports. Each model call or tool call becomes a checkpointed step that retries on its own. Progress goes to the workflow stream, and `getRun(id).getReadable({ startIndex })` lets any tab reconnect and replay from the start, even after closing the site.
- **One shared read-only tool registry** used by chat, the artifact builder and the widget renderer. Any read tool added to chat automatically becomes available to artifacts. Net worth history and budgets get added as new sources.

## The core idea

An artifact becomes **one agent conversation that owns two outputs**:

- **The Page:** free HTML in a sandbox, as today, with a better default design.
- **The Home card:** rendered natively in the app.

The same chat edits either one, and the agent works out which from what you say ("show this as well on Home" changes the card). Each output keeps its own version history with undo.

## How the Home card renders: three tiers, chosen by the AI

| Tier | What the AI produces | Runs where | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Preset** | One of the 6 templates plus data links | Our React, on the server | Most cards |
| **2. Composed** | A JSON layout built from ~20 of our primitives (Stack, Row, Stat, Delta, BarList, LineChart, AreaChart, Donut, Heatmap, Table, Progress, Badge, Segmented, Select, Tabs, Empty…) | Our React, on the server | Cards that don't fit a preset. This is the "AI makes its own template" case, and it's still 100% native. |
| **3. React code** | TSX written by the AI, using our component kit | **Sandboxed iframe** with our real CSS, fonts and components loaded, at a fixed size | Truly bespoke visuals |

**On "it can make React code":** yes, but never running inside the app itself. Code there would have your session, so a bad generation or an instruction hidden in a transaction description could call any server action (move money, delete data). Tier 3 gets the native look by loading the same component kit inside the sandbox. In practice Tier 2 should cover almost everything; Tier 3 is the escape hatch.

**Tier choice:** the agent tries the tiers in order (preset, then composed, then code) and picks the first that fits the request. All tiers share one data contract.

## Interactivity on Home

- **Params.** A card can declare controls such as month, period (1M/3M/6M) or account. A change calls `GET /api/widgets/:id?month=2026-10`. The server checks the value against the declared allowed values, re-runs that card's queries, and re-renders it. Nothing is computed by the AI at view time.
- **Local interactions** need no server call: tabs between series already loaded, tooltips, hover.
- **Drill-through links.** Clicking a bar can open `/money/transactions?category=…`. Links can only go to an allowlist of app routes, which iframes can't do today.
- **Tier 3** gets the same params through `postMessage`, so the app stays in control of data.

## Data contract (how financial truth is kept)

- Each card stores its own **queries**, using the shared registry and rolling forward with time as today. Changing the Page never breaks the card.
- Data is linked to the card with **paths plus a small set of safe operations** (`top n`, `sum`, `share`, `delta vs previous`). These run in app code on bigint minor units, with no `eval`. The app does all money formatting.
- **Checked before saving:** the agent's draft runs against live data in a step. Every link must resolve, the text must fit the chosen size (an overflow check from a server render), and empty or error states must be defined. A failed check goes back to the agent with the error, up to N times.

## Architecture

**Durable agent (Workflow `artifactAgent`):**
- Each turn starts a run: load the thread, call the model in a loop, run tools as steps, save.
- Tools:
  - every shared read tool
  - `write_page(html, queries)`
  - `write_card(tier, spec | tsx, queries, params, sizes)`
  - `check_card` (runs it live and reports the check results)
  - `ask_user` (clarifying questions)
- Progress events go to the workflow stream, so you can reconnect from anywhere. A small "Building…" pill in the app shell shows runs still active.

**Data model (fresh tables, no migration of old artifacts):**
- `artifacts`: id, title, thread state
- `artifact_messages`: the chat
- `artifact_pages`: versioned HTML and queries
- `artifact_cards`: versioned tier, spec/tsx, queries, params, allowed sizes, default size
- `artifact_runs`: workflow run id and status
- Home layout entries become `{ key, size }`, so built-in cards can be resized too. A pinned card points at a specific card version: chat edits create drafts, and **"Update on Home"** publishes one, so Home never changes without you seeing the change.

**Rendering:**
- `lib/widgets/primitives/*` is the component catalog. It is used both by the native renderer and, bundled, as the Tier 3 sandbox kit.
- `lib/widgets/spec.ts` holds the Zod schemas for Tiers 1–2, sizes and params.
- Home renders cards inside Suspense on the server. Tier 3 cards render as fixed-size frames. Sizes are fixed grid slots (S 2×1, M 3×1, L 4×1, XL 6×1) with a fixed height and no scrolling.
- The preview in the artifact's "Home card" tab uses **the same Home grid component** with your real neighbouring cards, so what you see is exactly what you get.

**Page design:**
- A **Moneo kit** is injected into the sandbox: CSS classes for cards, stats, eyebrows and grids, chart colours, and a chart helper.
- Default prompt: "use the kit unless the user asks for a specific style". When the user asks for a style, it wins.
- The Mercury design text in the examples gets removed.

## Build order (each phase a few commits)

1. Shared read-tool registry and the missing sources.
2. Builder on Workflow with a resumable stream, plus the chat thread and new tables.
3. Primitives, the Tier 1 and 2 renderer, fixed sizes and layout `{key, size}`.
4. The Home card tab, live preview, draft and publish.
5. Params, server re-render and drill-through links.
6. The Page design kit and prompt.
7. The Tier 3 sandbox with the bundled kit (optional, last).

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Tier 3 React code:** include it in the first version, or ship Tiers 1–2 first and add it only if we hit a real gap? I'd ship 1–2 first.
2. **Updating Home:** chat edits stay as drafts until you press "Update on Home", or go straight to Home? I'd use drafts.
3. **Multiple cards per artifact:** allow it (e.g. a "Subscriptions" artifact giving a total card and a next-charges card), or one card each? I'd allow several, since it costs little in this design.

## Yes: render the AI's React on our server, not in the browser

AI-written card code gets the freedom of Tier 3 and the speed and native look of Tiers 1–2. It runs **once on the server inside a real sandbox**. The browser only receives a safe element tree, which our own React draws directly in the Home grid. There is no iframe, and no AI JavaScript ever runs in the browser.

| | Sandboxed iframe (earlier plan) | **Server-rendered sandbox (new)** |
|---|---|---|
| Speed on Home | An extra request per card, plus a skeleton, plus loading charts from a CDN | Same as built-in cards: rendered with the page, cached |
| Looks native | Close, because we load our kit into it | **Identical**: it's real DOM inside our grid with our fonts and theme, and dark mode needs no reload |
| Freedom | Full | Full JSX, multiple charts, free layout, custom SVG, scoped CSS and animations |
| Safety | Good (isolated origin) | Stronger: the AI's code never runs in the browser |
| Can't do | — | Arbitrary client JavaScript such as canvas animation or live slider maths. Those are rare on Home; see the last decision below. |

## How it works

1. The card agent writes `card.tsx`: a pure function `Card({ data, params, size })`. It can use plain HTML, SVG and our kit components (`<Kit.BarList>`, `<Kit.Chart option={…}>`, `<Kit.Tabs>`, `<Kit.Segmented>`, `<Kit.Link>`, `<Kit.Tooltip>`…).
2. **When saved**, esbuild compiles it to plain JS. esbuild is already in `node_modules`.
3. **When rendered**, the code runs in **QuickJS (WASM)**, which is also already in `node_modules`. The sandbox has no network, filesystem, environment variables or clock, with limits of about 50 ms and 32 MB. Its input is only that card's query results. Its output is a JSON tree such as `{type:"div", props, children}`.
4. **On the host**, the tree is checked against an allowlist. Our server React then renders it: kit nodes become our real components, and text is escaped by React. Charts run through our own ECharts (v6, already a dependency), so the AI gets full ECharts styling but passes only option *data* and no functions.
5. Results are **cached** by card version, params and a hash of the data. Home pays for the sandbox only when the data has changed, and even then it costs tens of milliseconds per card, with cards rendered in parallel.

**Interactivity:**
- Interactive pieces are **our** client components: tabs, toggles, tooltips, hover, and drill-through links checked against an allowlist of app routes.
- Tabs render every panel up front and switch instantly.
- Changing a param (month, period, account) re-runs that card's queries plus the sandbox on the server, about 100 ms.

## Safety layers

1. **Code:** it runs only in QuickJS on the server, under time and memory limits, with no outside access.
2. **Data:** the card sees only its saved queries, which respect your AI data scopes.
3. **Output:**
   - an allowlist of HTML and SVG elements and attributes, with no `script`, `on*`, `iframe` or `foreignObject`
   - a limit on the number of nodes
   - links only to app routes
   - images only as `data:`
4. **CSS:**
   - `lightningcss` (already present) scopes every selector and `@keyframes` to the card and strips `url()` and `@import`
   - inline styles go through a property allowlist
   - `position: fixed` is not allowed

## Artistic freedom

- The card designer gets our kit and design tokens as defaults, but can ignore them when you ask for a specific look: gradients, illustrations drawn in SVG, custom typography using our font stack, animated rings, several charts in one card.
- The size (S/M/L/XL) is passed in as a prop, so one card can lay itself out differently at each size.

## Final plan, with your last message folded in

**The agent is the chat itself:**
- An artifact gets its own conversation, which runs through `/api/chat` with the artifact tools added.
- So it has **all chat tools** plus chat's durability: the `chat_requests` row, `after()`, resuming when you reopen, cancel, steer, the mic and attachments.
- Saved queries can use any read tool.

**Artifact tools:**
- `write_page(brief, queries)` and `write_card_code(brief, queries, params, sizes)` hand off to the designer model and include the current version when editing.
- The 6 presets are tools (`card_stat`, `card_bar_list`, …). They are pre-written `card.tsx` files in our repo and run natively with no sandbox.
- The agent uses a preset if one fits. Otherwise it uses the card-code skill, which is the default for anything with several parts or charts.

**Edit, don't duplicate:**

| Edit | New | Remove |
|---|---|---|
| `conversations` gets `artifact_id`; chat route gets artifact tools; `maxDuration` → 300 | `artifact_cards` (versioned: preset or code, compiled JS, queries, params, sizes) | `POST /api/artifacts` builder and `artifact_builds` with its builds UI and polling |
| `artifact-data.ts` → shared read-tool registry taken from the chat tools | `lib/cards/` (kit, QuickJS runner, sanitizer, renderer) | `MONEO_VIEW` widget path, `fit` sizing, `artifact-prompt.tsx` (replaced by the chat input) |
| Artifact viewer → chat panel with Page and Home card tabs | `GET /api/cards/[id]?params` | Mercury design prompt in the examples |
| `dashboard_layouts.items` → `{key, size}`; `setArtifactOnHome` → `setCardOnHome(card, size)` | | |
| Page frame route and `ArtifactFrame` stay for the full Page | | |

**About chat's durability:** it also dies on a deploy or crash mid-run, because it's `after()`-based. Artifacts will match chat exactly. Moving both to Workflow is a separate, later upgrade.

## Last decisions

1. **Cards that need live client JavaScript** (e.g. a what-if slider computed in the browser): skip them on Home, or allow a rare sandboxed "live card" iframe fallback? I'd skip them for now. A slider can trigger a server re-render with a short delay, and that's fast enough.
2. **Draft vs publish:** chat edits to a pinned card stay as drafts until you press "Update on Home"? I'd say yes.
3. **Several cards per artifact:** yes?

You are reviewing an architecture PLAN (no code yet) for the Moneo repo in your working directory (Next.js 16 + React 19 + TS personal-finance app, Supabase/Postgres, Vercel AI SDK, Vercel Workflow). Read AGENTS.md first. Do NOT edit any files and do not commit; this is a read-only review. Read the code as needed to verify claims.

Goal: tell us whether this plan is right for our needs, and find (1) loopholes/bugs in the design, (2) security problems, (3) simpler ways to get the same result, (4) better ways. Be concrete: cite files/lines, give a failure scenario for each problem, and a proposed fix. Rank findings by severity. If a part of the plan is good, say so in one line; don't pad. The app currently has one user (the developer), so backward compatibility / migrating old artifacts is NOT a constraint.

## Context: what exists today (verify)
- Artifacts = AI-built interactive HTML pages over the user's finance data. Builder: `app/api/artifacts/route.ts` (generateText + tools from `ARTIFACT_SOURCES` in `lib/ai/artifact-data.ts`, save_artifact tool, runs in `after()`, status in `artifact_builds` table). Page renders in a sandboxed iframe from `app/ai/artifacts/[id]/frame/route.ts` with a strict CSP (`ARTIFACT_FRAME_CSP`), data injected as `window.MONEO_DATA` from saved read-only queries that re-run on each open (dates roll forward).
- "Add to Home" (`app/dashboard-actions.ts` setArtifactOnHome, `lib/finance/dashboard.ts`, `app/page.tsx`) pins the same HTML as an iframe in `view=widget` mode (`components/artifact-frame.tsx`, `fit` auto-height 160–560px). The user is unhappy: widget is an afterthought of one HTML doing two views, heights vary/scroll, no preview before pinning, iframe per card is slow and not native-looking.
- Artifact data sources are a subset of chat's read tools (chat in `app/api/chat/route.ts` also has finance_detail, finance_entities, finance_scenario, forecast_evaluate, wealth_list, agents_findings, etc.).
- Chat durability: `chat_requests` row (running/completed/failed/canceled), `after()` keeps the run alive when the tab closes, reopening a conversation finds the running request; steer/cancel exist. Not Workflow-based.

## The plan to review
1. **Agent = the chat itself.** Each artifact gets its own conversation (`conversations.artifact_id`), running through `/api/chat` with extra artifact tools, so it has ALL chat tools and chat's durability (chat_requests, after(), resume on reopen, cancel, steer, mic, attachments). Raise chat `maxDuration` to 300. Saved artifact/card queries can reference any read tool via a shared read-only tool registry extracted from chat tools (replacing `ARTIFACT_SOURCES`), and re-run on each view with roll-forward dates.
2. **Artifact tools:** `write_page(brief, queries)` and `write_card_code(brief, queries, params, sizes)` delegate to a designer model (settings `ai_models.artifacts`), given the current version when editing. Six preset card tools (`card_stat`, `card_stat_row`, `card_bar_list`, `card_trend`, `card_progress`, `card_list`) = pre-written trusted card components in our repo, filled with data bindings; agent uses a preset if it fits, else the card-code "skill" (default for multi-part / multi-chart cards). The full Page stays sandboxed-iframe HTML, with an injected Moneo CSS kit as default design (user-requested styles override).
3. **Home cards from AI code, rendered server-side, no iframe:**
   - Designer writes `card.tsx`: pure function `Card({ data, params, size })` using plain HTML, SVG and kit components (`Kit.BarList`, `Kit.Chart option={...}`, `Kit.Tabs`, `Kit.Segmented`, `Kit.Link`, `Kit.Tooltip`, ...). No hooks/effects.
   - On save, compile with esbuild. On render, run in QuickJS (quickjs-emscripten, WASM) with no network/fs/env/clock, ~50ms / 32MB limits; input = only that card's query results; output = a JSON element tree `{type, props, children}`.
   - Host validates the tree against an allowlist (HTML+SVG elements/attrs; no script, on*, iframe, foreignObject; node cap; links only to allowlisted app routes; images only data:), maps kit nodes to our real React components (client components for tabs/tooltips/hover/drill links), renders with React (text auto-escaped). Charts: AI passes ECharts option DATA only (no functions), rendered by our own ECharts (v6, already a dep).
   - CSS: lightningcss scopes selectors and @keyframes to the card, strips url()/@import; inline styles via a property allowlist; no position:fixed.
   - Cache rendered tree keyed by (card version, params, data hash).
   - Interactivity: tabs pre-render all panels and switch client-side; params (month/period/account) declared with allowed values -> `GET /api/cards/[id]?params` re-runs that card's queries + sandbox (~100ms). No arbitrary client JS on Home (no live-slider maths in browser); sliders debounce a server re-render.
4. **UX:** artifact page = chat panel + tabs "Page" / "Home card". Home card tab previews the card inside the real Home grid component with real neighbours and live data, size chips S/M/L/XL (fixed grid slots 2/3/4/6 cols, fixed height, no scroll; size passed as prop). Chat edits to a pinned card create a draft; "Update on Home" publishes a specific card version. Several cards per artifact allowed.
5. **Data model:** keep `artifacts`, `artifact_versions` (page). New versioned `artifact_cards` (artifact_id, version, kind preset|code, source tsx, compiled js, queries, params, sizes, published flag/version). `dashboard_layouts.items` becomes `{key, size}`. Remove: `POST /api/artifacts` builder, `artifact_builds` + builds UI/polling, `MONEO_VIEW` widget path, `fit` sizing, `artifact-prompt.tsx`, Mercury design prompt in `lib/ai/artifact-examples.ts`.

## Specifically check
- Security of running AI-written code in QuickJS on the server inside a Next.js route (escape risk, DoS, memory, prompt-injection from transaction text into the code or tree, tree/prop injection into our kit components, CSS exfiltration/overlay/clickjacking within the Home page, link/redirect abuse, ECharts option fields that accept HTML strings or functions like tooltip.formatter/rich text, SVG attack surface like <use href>, <animate> attribute tricks, xlink:href, style injection).
- Whether "agent = chat route" is actually a good fit (chat maxDuration, model choice, tool count/prompt bloat, long HTML generation inside a chat turn, how a designer sub-call reports progress, cancellation mid designer call).
- Whether saved queries over ALL read tools is safe/stable (scopes, tools that need entity ids, pagination cursors, tools whose output includes evidence links, cost/latency on Home with N cards).
- Caching correctness (data hash, per-user isolation, theme, params) and Home load performance.
- Is QuickJS actually needed vs a simpler approach (e.g. AI emits the JSON tree directly / JSX string parsed without execution / a constrained template language)? Compare honestly on freedom, speed, safety, complexity.
- Anything in the draft/publish, versioning, or layout `{key,size}` design that breaks.

Output: a ranked findings list (severity, problem, failure scenario, fix), then a short "simpler/better alternatives" section, then a verdict (adopt as-is / adopt with changes / rethink) in one paragraph. Keep it tight.

I've started a GPT 6.1 Sol reviewer on the plan: [Review artifact Home-card architecture plan](<t3-thread://v2/88042f69-c439-49f6-a4b9-1fb5180f2502/thread:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3Aeb801510-d879-4c5f-a2ce-741f41c223ae%3Adelegate-task%3A06f357c5-c217-4950-a1e3-ed345f305bf8>). It's still running.

It's only reading code, not editing anything. I asked it to look for:
- design loopholes
- security problems: the QuickJS sandbox, prompt injection from transaction text, CSS and SVG tricks, chart settings that accept code or HTML
- whether running the artifact agent through chat is a good fit
- whether saved queries can safely use every read tool
- whether the cache can serve wrong or stale data
- simpler alternatives to QuickJS

I took your answers as my three recommendations: no live browser JavaScript on Home (sliders ask the server to redraw), chat edits stay drafts until "Update on Home", and an artifact can have several cards. When the review comes back I'll give you its findings and the plan with those changes applied, so you can sign off before I build.

Delegated task node:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3Aeb801510-d879-4c5f-a2ce-741f41c223ae%3Adelegate-task%3A06f357c5-c217-4950-a1e3-ed345f305bf8 (Review artifact Home-card architecture plan) [completed]:
**Adopt with changes.** Separating Page from Home cards, using trusted presets, previewing in the real grid, and publishing explicit versions are good decisions. The weakest part is introducing a general code runtime and broad rendering surface before defining their security contracts.

Ranked findings follow. References identify existing behavior; proposed components have no code yet.

1. **High — “JSON only” does not make kit props or ECharts safe.**  
   Existing artifacts have an opaque-origin sandbox ([artifact-data.ts:97](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:97)); native cards lose that boundary. A transaction description could prompt the designer to emit malicious chart options, which bypass HTML-element validation through `Kit.Chart`. ECharts explicitly documents raw HTML in `tooltip.formatter` and URL handling in `title.link`; banning functions is insufficient. [Official security guidance](https://echarts.apache.org/handbook/en/best-practices/security/).  
   **Fix:** strict schemas per kit component, rejecting unknown props. Prefer a small chart specification compiled into options by trusted code. Own tooltip rendering, links, images, toolbox actions, and event handlers. Never spread arbitrary props into React components; reject `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `srcDoc`, executable URLs, and prototype-related keys recursively.

2. **High — CSS scoping is not containment.**  
   Today’s frame cannot style Home; the proposed native card can. Scoped descendants with absolute positioning, extreme dimensions, negative margins, transforms or high stacking order can cover neighbours. SVG references/animation and URL-bearing presentation attributes create additional paths outside a simple `on*` filter.  
   **Scenario:** a generated “account verification” overlay captures clicks over the real dashboard.  
   **Fix:** trusted positioned, clipped, isolated card wrappers; bounded dimensions and stacking; curated style tokens instead of arbitrary CSS initially. Use a minimal SVG subset, excluding animation, `use`, external references and arbitrary `style`; namespace permitted IDs. Restrict data images by MIME type and byte size, preferably to raster formats. Build links from typed route IDs and owned entity IDs; do not accept arbitrary URLs merely because their pathname looks internal.

3. **High — QuickJS limits do not bound the whole request.**  
   Compilation, input serialization, output extraction, validation and chart rendering happen outside the proposed 50ms execution budget. Large inputs or output strings can exhaust host memory before the node cap is checked. Concurrent cards multiply this cost. QuickJS provides runtime memory, stack and interrupt controls, but those are distinct controls, not a total request budget. [Runtime documentation](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten/blob/main/doc/quickjs-emscripten-core/classes/QuickJSRuntime.md).  
   **Fix:** if retaining execution, use a killable worker/process with bounded concurrency and total deadlines; cap source, input/output bytes, depth, strings, chart points and compilation resources. Disable imports and all host capabilities; use an explicit JSX-to-tree runtime, never execute generated modules in Node. Benchmark WASM cold starts before promising ~100ms.

4. **High — Reusable read tools need a narrower contract than chat tools.**  
   Existing saved queries validate inputs, enforce scopes and strip internal evidence ([artifact-data.ts:36–53](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:36)). Chat additionally refreshes authorization around execution ([chat route:155–166](app/api/chat/route.ts:155)). Extracting closures or exposing every nominally read tool risks losing these properties. “Read-only” also includes expensive scenarios and context-dependent detail/pagination results.  
   **Scenario:** a saved recurring-series cursor becomes stale, or a card repeatedly evaluates a costly scenario on every Home load.  
   **Fix:** share underlying read services, but require explicit `persistable` adapters with schemas, required scopes, owned-ID checks, output projection, cost limits and date/pagination semantics. Recheck scopes on every view, including cache hits. Keep evidence URLs out of generic link props.

5. **High — Arbitrary card computation can violate financial truth.**  
   The current prompt already delegates display maths to generated code ([artifact builder:26](app/api/artifacts/route.ts:26)); moving that code onto Home makes misleading totals more authoritative. A card can convert large minor-unit strings to `Number`, combine currencies, or hard-code an amount while still passing every sandbox check.  
   **Fix:** application queries produce authoritative totals, currency groups and scenario results. Bind financial values through trusted formatting components. Keep generated transformations to presentation; label hypothetical results explicitly. A sandbox prevents capabilities, not incorrect arithmetic or invented claims.

6. **Medium — Chat reuse is sensible; raising `maxDuration` alone does not provide the proposed lifecycle.**  
   Chat currently has a **90-second model timeout** ([chat route:227](app/api/chat/route.ts:227)); the artifact builder allows 280 seconds and 32,000 output tokens ([artifact builder:89–91](app/api/artifacts/route.ts:89)). Cancellation is noticed at boundaries ([chat route:87–91](app/api/chat/route.ts:87)), so a nested designer call could continue and save after cancellation. `after()` preserves execution after disconnect, but is not crash-restart durability.  
   **Fix:** pass one deadline/cancellation contract through parent and designer; check request status immediately before saving. Persist designer-stage progress for reopening, and make saves idempotent by request/tool-call ID. Keep generated source out of ordinary chat history; return a version reference. Enable artifact tools only in artifact conversations, and give the designer only its necessary data/schema. Use Workflow only if restart/resume across process loss is required.

7. **Medium — Generic date rolling breaks semantic periods.**  
   Current logic shifts every nested `from`/`to` by elapsed days ([artifact-data.ts:68–90](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:68)). A “this month” card saved mid-month eventually displays a sliding interval rather than the current calendar month; historical comparisons may move unintentionally. Broader tools introduce more date meanings.  
   **Fix:** save explicit period expressions—current month, previous month, trailing days, fixed dates—and resolve them in the workspace timezone. Declare which fields accept parameter bindings; do not recursively rewrite arbitrary inputs.

8. **Medium — The cache misses the expensive work and omits render inputs.**  
   Computing a data hash requires fetching data first, so the proposed cache mostly saves sandbox execution. Existing queries fan out up to 12 calls per artifact ([artifact-data.ts:44](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:44), [89](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:89)); many cards can overwhelm Home. Omitting `size` gives incorrect trees after resizing.  
   **Fix:** batch/deduplicate normalized queries per workspace and render cards independently with bounded concurrency and failure states. Cache keys need card identity/version, workspace/user authorization context, normalized params, size, renderer version, and any consumed locale/timezone/theme settings. Keep HTTP responses private; use CSS variables for theme where possible. Treat latency targets as measurements to establish.

9. **Medium — Card identity and publication are underspecified.**  
   Current keys identify an artifact, allowing only one Home entry per artifact ([dashboard.ts:8–14](lib/finance/dashboard.ts:8)). A row containing both card versions and a `published` flag does not establish stable identity or atomic publication.  
   **Scenario:** editing one of several cards updates the wrong slot, or concurrent edits overwrite a newer draft/publication.  
   **Fix:** separate stable card IDs from immutable version rows; store one published-version pointer per card, updated transactionally with optimistic concurrency. Home keys identify cards; layout entries also need per-instance params if instances may differ. Preserve existing layout conflict checks ([dashboard-actions.ts:14–15](app/dashboard-actions.ts:14)). Scope conversation/card relationships to the workspace with RLS and constraints.

10. **Medium — Fixed heights need responsive and overflow rules.**  
    Existing layout validation accepts strings, with uniqueness and a 50-item limit ([dashboard.ts:11](lib/finance/dashboard.ts:11)). `{key,size}` requires coordinated database/schema/action/UI changes. Desktop spans of 2/3/4/6 alone do not define mobile behavior.  
    **Scenario:** long labels, zoom or larger fonts hide financial values and keyboard-focused controls in a clipped card.  
    **Fix:** define responsive spans, trusted content budgets, truncation rules and a reliable “Open page” action. Validate every supported size with realistic long/empty/error data; preview pinning against the exact published version.

**Simpler/better alternatives**

Start with a **versioned JSON card document**: trusted layout primitives, data bindings, bounded repetition/conditions, presets and a constrained chart schema. The AI writes this once; application code resolves bindings on each view. This supports multi-part cards without QuickJS, esbuild or a general CSS sanitizer.

Raw JSON trees alone cannot safely refresh hard-coded values; bindings are essential. Parsing JSX without execution still needs a constrained expression language for loops/calculations, so it mainly changes syntax. QuickJS offers substantially more computational freedom, but adds operational and security complexity that the stated Home requirements do not yet justify. Keep unrestricted interaction in the sandboxed Page and introduce executable cards only after a concrete limitation warrants them.

**Verdict:** adopt with changes: reuse chat orchestration, split Page/card versions, and implement explicit publication and native previews. Begin with declarative cards and curated persistable query adapters; defer QuickJS until the simpler renderer demonstrably cannot meet a real card requirement. This was a read-only architecture review; no files changed or tests run, and the proposed sandbox’s actual isolation and latency remain unverified.

The review's verdict is **adopt with changes**. It agrees with splitting Page from Home card, using the chat as the agent, previewing in the real Home grid, and publishing explicit versions. Its main point is that running AI-written code with QuickJS is the weakest part, and I think it's right.

## The big question: QuickJS vs a card document

Its argument is that the risk isn't really the code running; it's what the code outputs. Both approaches need the same safeguards, so QuickJS adds a runtime, esbuild, a CSS sanitizer and worker limits without solving the hard problems:

- **Chart settings can carry HTML and links.** ECharts accepts raw HTML in places like tooltip formatters and link fields, so even "data only, no functions" is open to injection. Every kit component needs a strict schema, and charts need our own small chart spec that trusted code turns into ECharts settings.
- **Card styles can cover the rest of Home.** Without an iframe, card CSS could draw a fake overlay over the real dashboard. Cards need a clipped, isolated wrapper plus a style allowlist.
- **Code can do money maths wrong.** It could combine currencies or lose precision with `Number`, and nothing in the sandbox would catch it. Totals have to come from app queries anyway, so the card code would only be doing layout.

If the code is only doing layout, the AI can write the same thing as a **JSON card document**:
- free nesting
- repeat over data
- shown/hidden when a list is empty
- multiple charts
- SVG shapes
- rich style tokens such as gradients and type sizes

**What it can't do is arbitrary calculation, which shouldn't live in a card anyway.** This is not "6 templates". The AI designs a whole card; it just writes it as data instead of JSX. The presets become saved documents.

**I'm changing my recommendation:** use the card document now, keep the full freedom of the Page in its iframe, and add QuickJS later only if a real card needs it. That's simpler and safer, and it's still native and fast.

## Fixes I'm taking regardless

- **Saved queries use explicit "persistable" adapters, not the raw chat tools.** Each adapter has a schema, scopes checked again on every view (including cache hits), checks that any ids belong to you, a cost limit, and no evidence links or pagination cursors.
- **Periods are saved as meaning, not shifted dates.** "Current month" or "last 90 days" is stored as that and resolved in your timezone. Today's code moves every date by the number of days elapsed, which turns "this month" into a sliding window.
- **The designer call shares the chat's deadline and cancel.** It checks status just before saving, saves only once per request, and progress is saved so a reopened tab sees it. Generated source stays out of the chat history (the chat only gets a version reference), and the artifact tools exist only in artifact conversations. One correction from the review: chat's model timeout is 90s, so raising `maxDuration` alone isn't enough.
- **Cards have stable ids, separate from immutable version rows.** Each card has one published-version pointer, updated with conflict checks. Home layout keys point to cards, not artifacts.
- **Home loads cheaply.** Repeated queries across cards are combined, cards render independently with a cap on how many run at once, and each card has its own error state. The cache key includes size, workspace, renderer version and timezone. Theme uses CSS variables, so the cache doesn't need it.
- **Fixed sizes come with rules.** Mobile column spans, limits on how much content each size holds, truncation, an "Open" link that's always visible, and preview tests with long, empty and error data.

## Your call

1. **Card document now, QuickJS only if needed later** (my recommendation, and the reviewer's), or **QuickJS code now with all the hardening above**?
2. Okay to go ahead and implement in phases, with a commit per step, once you pick?

## For you

- **One chat per artifact.** Every artifact is a conversation using the same chat, so it has all of chat's tools, the mic and attachments. It keeps running if you leave or close the site, and you find it in progress when you come back. You can cancel or steer it mid-build.
- **Two outputs, side by side:**
  - **Page:** the full interactive HTML (sliders, what-ifs). It uses our Moneo design kit by default and follows any style you ask for.
  - **Home card:** a compact native card.
- **Adding to Home:**
  1. You say "add to Home" or press the button.
  2. The **Home card** tab shows the card inside your real Home, next to your real cards, with live data.
  3. You pick a size: S, M, L or XL. Sizes have a fixed height and never scroll.
  4. You refine it in the same chat, e.g. "also show the yearly total" or "drop the chart".
  5. You press **Add to Home**.
- **Editing later:** chat changes to a card that's already on Home stay as a draft until you press **Update on Home**, so Home never changes without you seeing it first. Every version is kept and can be undone.
- **On Home:** cards look and load like Net worth or Briefing: no iframe and no skeleton flash, and dark mode just works. They're clickable: month or period switches, tabs, tooltips, and bars that open Transactions. One artifact can have several cards.

## How it works

- **Agent:** the chat route with artifact-only tools:
  - `write_page`: the designer model writes the HTML
  - `write_card`: the designer writes a card document
  - 6 preset card tools for common shapes
- **Card document:** JSON the AI designs freely: nested layout, repeated rows, multiple charts, SVG shapes, style tokens. Our server renders it with our own React components. No AI code ever runs.
- **Data:** each card and page saves queries through "persistable" read adapters that cover every chat read tool. Scopes are checked on every view, and periods are stored as meaning ("this month"), not as fixed dates. All money totals come from app code; cards only display them.
- **Safety:**
  - every component prop is checked against a strict schema
  - charts use our own chart spec, so no raw ECharts HTML or links
  - each card sits in a clipped, isolated box and can't draw over Home
  - links can only go to app routes
  - the Page keeps its sandboxed iframe
- **Speed:** queries repeated across cards run once, cards render in parallel and each has its own error state, and renders are cached by card version, size and data.

## Code changes

|---|---|---|
| Chat (artifact conversations and tools), artifact viewer (chat plus Page and Home card tabs), artifact data (adapters and period meaning), Home layout (`{card, size}`), frame route (Page only) | `artifact_cards` and card version tables with a published pointer, `lib/cards/` (document schema, renderer, kit), card data route | Old builder route, `artifact_builds` and its polling, widget mode in the HTML, auto-height iframes, old prompt box, Mercury design prompt |

**Later, only if needed:** AI-written React code in a sandbox, for card designs the document format can't express.

Agreed. Custom cards will be AI-written React, built with every safeguard the reviewer asked for. (The `write_card` document was meant as the "make its own" path, but React gives you more visual freedom.)

## How a card gets made

1. If one of the **6 presets** fits, the agent uses it. Presets are our own trusted code.
2. If none fits, the designer **writes its own React card** (`card.tsx`):
   - any layout, several charts, custom SVG art, its own styling and animations
   - a different layout for each size (S/M/L/XL)
   - the default for anything visual or with several parts

## How AI React runs safely and fast

- **Where it runs:** esbuild compiles it when saved. It then runs on the server in **QuickJS inside a worker that can be killed**:
  - no network, filesystem, environment variables, clock or imports
  - a hard total deadline
  - caps on code size, input and output size, tree depth and number of chart points
  - a limit on how many cards render at once
- **What it outputs:** an element tree, never HTML and never browser JavaScript. Our React renders it natively, so there's no iframe.
- **Checking the output:**
  - only allowed HTML and a safe subset of SVG (no `<use>`, animation tags, external references, `on*` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`)
  - images only as small `data:` rasters
  - every kit component has a strict prop schema that rejects anything unknown
- **Charts:** the card describes them with our own chart spec, and trusted code turns that into ECharts. No raw ECharts settings, so no HTML formatters or links get through.
- **Containment:** each card sits in an isolated, clipped wrapper (`contain: paint`, `overflow: clip`). Even absolutely positioned or animated content can't cover the rest of Home. Its CSS is scoped to the card, with `url()` and `@import` stripped.
- **Money:** the card can arrange and style figures but never computes them. Totals come from app queries and are shown through our `Kit.Money` component, and what-if values are labelled as estimates.
- **Links:** the card picks from typed app routes and your own ids, never free URLs.
- **Interactivity:** our own components handle tabs, toggles, tooltips and drill-through clicks. Changing a param re-renders that card on the server.
- **Cache:** results are cached by card version, size, params, data, timezone and renderer version. The sandbox runs only when something changes.

Everything else in the summary stays the same: chat as the durable agent with all tools, Page and Home card tabs, live preview in your real Home, drafts until "Update on Home", several cards per artifact, versioning and undo, and the code changes listed.

One honest caveat: QuickJS speed is a guess until I benchmark it. I'll measure that first. If it's too slow, I'll keep the same design and switch the engine.

Moneo · artifacts & Home cardsArchitectureA card's lifeRenderingSafetyDataDecisionsTested liveLimits

Moneo · personal finance · artifacts

Build it from your data, then live with it on Home.

An artifact is a page Moneo builds from your real finances, in its own chat. Any part of it can become a card on your Home: previewed in place, sized, published when you're happy, and drawn by the app itself — not an iframe. The model can design anything, but every number still comes from the app.

~1 msto run a busy card's code in the sandbox (warm)
0lines of AI code that run in your browser
1 chatbuilds the page and every card, with all chat tools
~1.5 sHome with a published card, production build

Architecture

One chat, two outputs, one data contract

The artifact's chat is the normal Moneo chat with four extra tools. A designer model writes the Page (HTML) or a card (React). The app saves the queries the work needs, never the numbers, and reruns them every time anything is shown.

A card's life

From “add this to Home” to a card you can trust

Every step is a normal chat request, so it keeps going if you close the tab and shows as working when you come back.

1 · ask

Say it in the chat

“Add a small card with last month's total and top categories, with a month switch.”

2 · read

The agent reads real data

It uses the same read tools as chat, then writes queries with dates as meaning (@param:month.from), never fixed dates.

3 · design

Preset or its own React

If one of six shapes fits, it fills a preset. Otherwise a designer writes the card's own TSX, with any layout, several charts or custom SVG.

4 · check

Rendered before it's saved

It's compiled and run at S, M, L and XL with live data, and the tree is checked. Failures go back to the designer up to 3 times.

5 · preview

A draft, in place

The Home cards tab shows it in its Home slot between your own widgets, live and interactive. Pick a size, then ask for changes.

6 · publish

You decide when Home changes

Add to Home publishes that exact version. Later edits are drafts until “Update on Home”, and every version is kept to go back to.

Rendering

AI-written React that never runs in your browser

The card's code runs once on the server inside QuickJS, a JavaScript engine compiled to WASM. Its only output is a tree of plain data, { type, props, children }. The app checks that tree and draws it with its own React, so it gets your fonts and theme, switches dark mode instantly, and has no iframe.

Measured (benchmark script in the repo)

9 mscompile TSX → JS (sucrase), once at save
44 msfirst render; the WASM engine starts
1.1 mswarm render p50 (p95 2.9 ms): two charts, 12 rows
7 ms8 cards at once

The cost on Home is the data queries, which every widget already pays. Cards on one Home share reads: the same query runs once.

What a card can use

HTML and SVG (gradients, filters, clip paths), style objects, and scoped CSS with :hover, @keyframes and @media. The kit, which the app draws:

Kit.MoneyKit.ChartKit.TabsKit.ParamKit.LinkKit.Style

Tabs switch instantly in the browser. A Param (month, period or choice) re-renders the card on the server with new data in about 100 ms. Links are built by the app from a typed target.

Safety

Five walls between the model and your Home

The model writes the code, and text in your transactions could try to steer it, so we treat both the code and its output as untrusted.

LayerWhat it stops
QuickJS sandboxfresh runtime per renderNo network, files, env, timers or imports. A 1 s deadline and a 64 MB memory ceiling stop a runaway loop from stalling Home; they aren't design limits.
Tree checkallowlistOnly known HTML/SVG elements and attributes get through: no script, iframe, img, a, use, foreignObject, event handlers or dangerouslySetInnerHTML. No url() except to the card's own namespaced ids, so data can't leave through a stylesheet.
Kit schemasstrict Zod per componentUnknown props are refused. Charts take numbers and labels only, never chart-library options that accept HTML or functions. Links take a typed page plus ids, never a URL.
Scoped CSSpostcssEvery selector is prefixed with the card, keyframes are renamed, @import and url() are dropped, and < is escaped so CSS can't close its own style tag.
Containmentthe app's wrapperA fixed height with overflow: clip, contain: layout paint style and isolation. Even position: fixed stays inside the card, so it can't draw a fake overlay over Home.

Data

Numbers come from the app, and they stay current

persistable reads

Every chat read tool, behind an adapter

Investigate, cashflow, transactions, detail, scenario, entities, balances, accounts, recurring, goals, wealth, forecast and agent findings. Each declares its input schema and AI scopes, which are checked again on every view. Output is made readable (formatted money, names for ids) with internal evidence stripped.

dates as meaning

“This month” stays this month

Queries save tokens such as @month_start, @days_ago:29 and @param:month.from, resolved in your timezone each view. A literal date is refused unless you asked for a fixed past period. The old approach shifted saved dates by elapsed days, so “this month” slowly became a sliding window.

params

Controls can't widen what a card reads

A request can only pick a declared option: one of the last N months, a listed period, or a listed choice. Anything else falls back to the default.

financial truth

Designers don't do money maths

Totals come from their own query. Cards show money as the app's formatted strings or through Kit.Money, which uses bigint minor units. Minor amounts become numbers only for bar lengths.

Decisions

What we could have built, and why we didn't

OptionWhy not (or why)
Keep one HTML doing two viewsthe old widgetNo. The widget was an afterthought of the page, an iframe of varying height that scrolled, loaded charts from a CDN and reloaded on theme change. And you couldn't see it on Home before pinning.
Card iframe with our CSS kitsandboxed, fixed sizeNo. It's safe, but it's an extra request, document and skeleton per card, and it still isn't native DOM.
JSON card document onlyreviewer's suggestionNot alone. It's simpler and safe, but caps how expressive a card can be. We kept its safety ideas (strict schemas, typed links, money through trusted components) and let the AI write real React.
Run AI React in the pagefastest to buildNever. The code would run with your session and could call any server action.
AI React in QuickJS on the serverchosenYes. It's as free as code, as fast and native as built-in widgets, and no AI code reaches the browser. The six presets go through the same pipeline from trusted source.
A separate artifact builderthe old routeReplaced. The artifact's chat is the chat, which gives it every read tool, durability, steering, cancel, the mic and attachments at no extra cost. Its build tracker table is gone.
Vercel Workflow for buildsNot now. Artifacts match chat exactly (after() + a request row). Surviving a deploy or crash mid-run is a later upgrade for both.

Tested live

What real runs found that unit tests didn't

bundling

The WASM moved

The production build copied QuickJS's WASM file to a path that didn't exist at runtime. Fix: load the sandbox packages from node_modules (serverExternalPackages). The card e2e test now runs against next start.

frozen dates

Six queries for six months

The first month switch came back as six queries with literal dates, so it would have frozen at November. Fix: a month param with tokens, and literal dates refused unless intended.

empty sample

Guessing field names

On the 1st of the month the sample data was empty, so the designer guessed row.categoryName and every bar read “Uncategorized”. Fix: it now also sees another option's data (last month) as a shape reference.

money

Hand-made totals

The designer summed amounts and formatted them itself. Fix: totals come from their own query, and money is shown only as app-formatted values.

Limits

What still isn't perfect

No live browser maths on Home

A slider on a card asks the server to re-render, which is fast but not 60 fps. The Page (sandboxed iframe) keeps full client-side interactivity.

Durability equals chat's

A deploy or crash mid-build loses that run. The request shows as failed, and you ask again.

A designer can still mislabel

The sandbox stops capabilities, not wrong labels. The preview, drafts and version history are how you catch and undo that.

Tailwind classes

Only classes the app already uses exist, so designed cards style themselves with style objects and scoped CSS.

Principles

The rules behind every decision

Money facts come from code

Pages and cards save queries, not numbers. Totals and formatting come from the app.

Untrusted by default

AI code runs only in a sandbox, and its output is checked before it reaches React.

See it where it will live

The preview is the real card in its Home slot. Home changes only when you publish.

Reuse, don't fork

One chat and one set of read tools. Presets and designed cards share one render pipeline.
